hero.name: Malini
hero.who: the owner of a tiffin service in Chennai whose hardworking team pulls in different directions

story.b: Malini's tiffin service in Velachery started in her own kitchen five years ago. Now she has six staff, two delivery boys and two hundred daily customers, mostly office workers along the IT corridor. Everyone works hard. Selvi in the kitchen keeps trying new recipes. Karthik on deliveries is chasing speed. Her nephew Vignesh is busy making social media posts. Malini herself spends nights on accounts and mornings on complaints. Yet monthly customers keep leaving, and nobody can say why. One Saturday evening, after a long day, she asks the team what the most important goal is this month. She gets five different answers, and one person just shrugs.

ask.q: Malini's team works hard but has five different ideas of what matters. What should she do first?
o: Ask everyone to work even harder on their own tasks
Agree together on one clear goal and how they will know they reached it
Hire more staff so all the different goals can be covered
ask.why: Hard work pulling in different directions cancels itself out. One shared goal with clear signs of success points everyone the same way. Working harder only speeds up the confusion, and more staff just adds more directions. Clarity first, then effort.

chapters.take: Hard work counts most when everyone knows which goal it serves.

story.b: Malini sits down with a notebook and tries a new way to write goals. First, what does she want, in words that excite her? She writes: become the tiffin that office workers never want to leave. Then, how will she know it is happening? She writes three things she can count: keep most monthly customers for a second month, cut late deliveries to under five a week, and get thirty new customers through referrals. Reading it back, she feels the team will understand this far better than a vague call to do better. On Monday morning she reads it out over filter coffee, and Selvi asks which of her new recipes will help.

ask.q: Karthik writes his goal as just better deliveries, with nothing else. How can Malini help him make it useful?
o: Leave it as it is, since everyone knows what better means
Make it longer, with a detailed list of every daily task
Keep the aim, and add a few numbers that show when he has achieved it
ask.why: A good goal pairs an inspiring aim with a few measurable signs, like on-time deliveries each week. Without numbers, better means something different to everyone. A long task list buries the aim under chores, so it guides daily work less, not more.

chapters.take: Pair an inspiring aim with a few results you can actually measure.

story.b: Once the team starts thinking about goals, ideas pour in. Vignesh wants a mobile app. Selvi wants to launch a payasam and dessert line. A customer asks if they can cater her cousin's wedding for four hundred guests. Karthik suggests a second kitchen in Tambaram. Every idea sounds good, and the old Malini would have said yes to all of them. This time she pins the goal sheet to the kitchen wall and asks one question about each idea. Does it help customers stay? The wedding money is tempting, but it would pull the whole team away for a week. She keeps three goals for the quarter and says not now to the rest.

ask.q: Vignesh lists eight goals for his social media work this month. What should Malini advise?
o: Pick the top two or three and drop the rest for now
Keep all eight, since aiming high is always good
Add a few more goals so nothing is missed
ask.why: Too many goals scatter effort until nothing gets done well. Choosing two or three forces the hard choice about what matters most. Keeping all eight looks ambitious but spreads him thin, and adding more makes the problem worse. Focus means deciding what you will not do.

chapters.take: Focus means choosing a few goals and saying not now to the rest.

story.b: Malini draws a big chart on chart paper and sticks it beside the kitchen door, where everyone passes. At the top is the main goal. Below it, each person writes their own goal in their own handwriting, even the delivery boys. Within a week, something surprising happens. Karthik sees that Selvi's goal is to finish cooking by eleven, while his is to leave by eleven fifteen. They realise that packing, squeezed in between, is where the delays happen. Together they move two staff to packing at ten forty-five. Vignesh notices the referral goal and starts adding a small thank-you card for every customer who brings a friend.

ask.q: Malini's friend, who manages a clinic, keeps her team's goals in a private file only she sees. What would Malini suggest?
o: Keep them private so nobody feels judged
Share them openly so the team can spot overlaps and help each other
Share them only with the best performers
ask.why: When goals are visible, people see how their work connects and where they can help, as Karthik and Selvi did. Private goals leave everyone guessing. Sharing only with a few creates an inner circle and hides the very overlaps that cause trouble.

chapters.take: Goals everyone can see become goals everyone can help with.

story.b: Every Friday afternoon, the team scores each goal honestly. In the third week, late deliveries are still at nine a week, and the chart makes it impossible to pretend otherwise. They find the cause quickly: one route through Madipakkam jams badly after rain. Karthik changes the route order. By week six, late deliveries are down to four. The referral goal is harder. Malini set thirty on purpose, knowing it was bold. They are at fourteen, and Vignesh looks discouraged. Malini reminds the team which goals are must-do and which are stretch. On-time delivery is a promise to customers. Thirty referrals was always meant to push them past safe thinking.

ask.q: At the end of the quarter, the team reaches twenty-two of its thirty referrals. How should Malini see this?
o: As a failure, since they missed the target
As proof the target was silly and should be dropped
As good progress on a stretch goal, worth celebrating and learning from
ask.why: A stretch goal is meant to be bold, so reaching most of it often beats fully hitting a timid one. Twenty-two new customers is real growth. Calling it a failure discourages the team, and dropping stretch targets means they stop reaching beyond safe thinking.

chapters.take: Track goals often, and know which ones are promises and which are stretches.

story.h: Ten minutes on the back steps
story.b: Malini notices the chart shows numbers, but not people. So she starts a short chat with each person every week, ten minutes over tea on the back steps. What went well, what is in the way, what do you need from me. In one chat, Selvi admits she is exhausted because her mother-in-law is unwell, which explains why her new recipes stopped. Malini shifts her hours for a month. In another, a delivery boy, Murugan, says his old phone keeps freezing on the map. Malini buys him a second-hand phone for the route. She also starts thanking people by name on Fridays, for small things the chart never shows.

ask.q: Malini's friend runs a bakery and plans one long staff review form per year. What would Malini suggest instead?
o: Short, regular chats about progress, roadblocks and wins
A longer form, so nothing in the year is missed
No talks at all, just the numbers on the chart
ask.why: Frequent short check-ins catch problems early, while there is still time to help, and regular thanks keep people motivated. A once-a-year form arrives too late to fix anything and is often dreaded. Numbers alone miss the human reasons behind them, like Selvi's tiredness.

chapters.take: Goals work best with regular, honest conversation, not just a scorecard.

story.b: Three months later, Malini's tiffin service has had its best quarter yet. Most customers stay for a second month, late deliveries are down to two or three a week, and twenty-two new customers came through friends. The dessert line and the second kitchen sit on a list marked later. The wedding catering never happened, and nobody misses it. On the first Monday of the new quarter, the team gathers by the kitchen door to draft the next chart. This time Malini does not write the main goal alone. Selvi suggests it, Karthik adds a number, and Vignesh insists on one bold stretch target. Everyone already knows which goals matter.

chapters.take: Clear, shared and regularly checked goals turn hard work into real progress.
